changes.before: Mellem os var der, som jeg allerede har sagt et sted, havets bånd. Foruden at holde vores hjerter sammen gennem lange adskillelser havde det den virkning at gøre os tolerante over for hinandens historier — og endda over for hinandens overbevisninger. Advokaten — den bedste af gamle fyre — havde, takket være sine mange år og mange dyder, den eneste pude på dækket og lå på det eneste tæppe. Bogholderen havde allerede taget en æske dominobrikker frem og legede arkitektonisk med brikkerne. Marlow sad med korslagte ben agterude, lænet mod mesanmasten. Han havde indfaldne kinder, en gul hudfarve, en rank ryg, et asketisk udtryk, og med armene sænkede og håndfladerne vendt udad lignede han et idol. Direktøren, der havde forvisset sig om, at ankeret holdt godt, gik agterud og satte sig blandt os. Vi udvekslede et par dovne ord. Derefter herskede der tavshed om bord på yachten. Af en eller anden grund kom vi aldrig i gang med det dominospil. Vi følte os meditative, og duede til intet andet end stille at stirre. Dagen sluttede i en ro af stille, udsøgt klarhed. Vandet skinnede fredeligt; himlen, uden en plet, var en mild umådelighed af ubesmittet lys; selv tågen over Essex-marsken var som et tyndt, strålende stof, ophængt fra de skovklædte stigninger inde i landet, og draperende de lave kyster i gennemsigtige folder. Kun dysterheden mod vest, der rugede over de øvre strækninger, blev mere sombre minut for minut, som vred over solens nærmen sig.
changes.after: Som jeg vist har sagt et andet sted, var vi knyttet sammen af havet. Det holdt vores hjerter tæt på hinanden gennem lange adskillelser og gjorde os overbærende med hinandens historier — selv med hinandens overbevisninger. Advokaten, den bedste gamle ven, man kunne ønske sig, havde i kraft af sine mange år og mange dyder fået den eneste pude på dækket og lå på det eneste tæppe. Bogholderen havde allerede taget en æske dominoer frem og morede sig med at bygge med benbrikkerne. Marlow sad med korslagte ben helt agterude, lænet mod mesanmasten. Han havde indfaldne kinder, gullig hud, rank ryg og et asketisk udseende. Med armene hængende ned og håndfladerne vendt udad lignede han et gudebillede. Da direktøren havde sikret sig, at ankeret holdt godt, gik han agterud og satte sig hos os. Vi vekslede dovent et par ord. Så blev der stille om bord på lystbåden. Af en eller anden grund kom vi ikke i gang med at spille domino. Vi var eftertænksomme og havde kun lyst til at sidde og se roligt ud over vandet. Dagen gik på hæld i en stilhed af udsøgt, rolig glans. Vandet skinnede fredeligt; den pletfri himmel var et mildt, umådeligt rum af rent lys. Selv tågen over Essex' marskland lignede et fint, strålende stof, som hang fra de skovklædte højdedrag inde i landet og lagde sig over de lave bredder i gennemsigtige folder. Kun mørket mod vest, som rugede over flodens øvre løb, blev dybere minut for minut, som om det blev vredt over, at solen nærmede sig.

changes.before: Med det samme indtraf en forandring over vandene, og roen blev mindre strålende men dybere. Den gamle flod hvilede uforstyrret i sin brede strækning ved dagens afslutning, efter århundreders gode tjeneste til den race, der befolkede dens bredder, udstrakt i den rolige værdighed af en vandvej, der førte til jordens yderste ender. Vi så på den ærværdige strøm, ikke i den levende rødme fra en kort dag, der kommer og går for evigt, men i det ophøjede lys fra varige minder. Og intet er lettere for en mand, der, som man siger, har »fulgt havet« med ærbødighed og hengivenhed, end at fremmane fortidens store ånd på Themsens nedre strækninger. Tidevandsstrømmen løber frem og tilbage i sin uophørlige tjeneste, fyldt med minder om mænd og skibe, den har båret til hjemmets hvile eller havets kampe. Den har kendt og tjent alle de mænd, som nationen er stolt af, fra Sir Francis Drake til Sir John Franklin, riddere alle, med og uden titel — de store omvandrende søfartsriddere. Den har båret alle de skibe, hvis navne er som juveler, der blinker i tidens nat, fra Golden Hind, der vendte hjem med sine rundede sider fulde af skatte for at blive besøgt af Hendes Majestæt Dronningen og således forsvinde ud af den gigantiske fortælling, til Erebus og Terror, som drog ud på andre erobringer — og som aldrig vendte tilbage. Den har kendt skibene og mændene. De sejlede fra Deptford, fra Greenwich, fra Erith — eventyrerne og kolonisterne; kongelige skibe og købmandsskibe; kaptajner, admiraler, de mørke »snyltehandlere« fra østhandelen og de officielt udnævnte »generaler« fra Ostindiske kompagniets flåder. Guldjægere eller efterstræbere af berømmelse, alle var de draget ud på den strøm, bærende sværdet, og ofte faklen, sendebud for magten inde i landet, bærere af en gnist fra den hellige ild. Hvilken storhed havde ikke flydt på den flods ebbe ind i mysteriet om en ukendt jord!... Menneskers drømme, samfunds frø, imperiers spirer.
changes.after: Straks ændrede vandet sig, og roen blev mindre strålende, men dybere. Den gamle flod lå uden krusninger i sit brede løb, mens dagen svandt, efter i umindelige tider at have tjent det folk, der beboede dens bredder. Den bredte sig med den stille værdighed, som tilkommer en vandvej til jordens fjerneste egne. Vi så på den ærværdige strøm, ikke i den levende glød fra en kort dag, der kommer og forsvinder for altid, men i varige minders ophøjede lys. Og for et menneske, der med respekt og kærlighed har »faret til søs«, som man siger, er intet lettere end at fremmane fortidens store ånd på Themsens nedre løb. Tidevandsstrømmen løber frem og tilbage i sin uophørlige tjeneste, fyldt med minder om mænd og skibe, som den har båret til hjemmets hvile eller havets kampe. Den havde kendt og tjent alle de mænd, nationen er stolt af, fra Sir Francis Drake til Sir John Franklin, riddere alle sammen, med og uden titel — havets store vandrende riddere. Den havde båret alle de skibe, hvis navne glimter som juveler i tidens nat: fra _Golden Hind_, der vendte hjem med sine runde flanker fulde af skatte, fik besøg af dronningen og dermed gled ud af den vældige fortælling, til _Erebus_ og _Terror_, som drog ud for at gøre andre erobringer — og aldrig kom tilbage. De var sejlet ud fra Deptford, fra Greenwich, fra Erith: eventyrerne og nybyggerne, kongernes skibe og børsmændenes skibe, kaptajner, admiraler, de lyssky »fribyttere« i handelen med Østen og de officielt udnævnte »generaler« for de ostindiske flåder. Om de jagtede guld eller berømmelse, var de alle draget ud ad den strøm med sværdet og ofte faklen, som budbringere for magten inde i landet, bærere af en gnist fra den hellige ild. Hvilken storhed var ikke drevet med denne flods ebbe ud i en ukendt jords mysterium! ... Menneskers drømme, frøene til samfund, spirerne til imperier.

changes.before: Han var den eneste af os, der stadig »fulgte havet«. Det værste, der kunne siges om ham, var, at han ikke repræsenterede sin klasse. Han var sømand, men han var også vandringsmand, mens de fleste sømænd lever, hvis man kan udtrykke det sådan, et stillesiddende liv. Deres sind er af den hjemmeblivende slags, og deres hjem er altid med dem — skibet; og det samme er deres land — havet. Et skib ligner meget et andet, og havet er altid det samme. I deres omgivelsers uforanderlighed glider de fremmede kyster, de fremmede ansigter, livets skiftende umådelighed forbi, sløret ikke af en fornemmelse af mysterium, men af en let nedladende uvidenhed; for der er intet mysteriøst for en sømand, medmindre det er havet selv, som er hans tilværelses elskerinde og lige så uudgrundelig som Skæbnen. Resten — efter arbejdstid er en tilfældig spadseretur eller en tilfældig druktur i land nok til at åbenbare for ham hemmeligheden ved et helt kontinent, og som regel finder han hemmeligheden ikke værd at vide. Sømandshistorier har en direkte enkelhed, hvis hele mening ligger inde i skallen på en knækket nød. Men Marlow var ikke typisk (hvis man ser bort fra hans tilbøjelighed til at fortælle historier), og for ham lå meningen med en episode ikke inde i den som en kerne, men uden om den, omsluttende fortællingen, der bragte den frem kun som et skær fremkalder en dis, i lighed med et af de tågede haloer, som undertiden bliver synlige ved måneskinnets spøgelsesagtige belysning.
changes.after: Han var den eneste af os, der stadig »fór til søs«. Det værste, man kunne sige om ham, var, at han ikke lignede sine standsfæller. Han var sømand, men også en vandrer, mens de fleste sømænd fører et stillesiddende liv, hvis man kan udtrykke det sådan. De er hjemmemennesker af sind, og hjemmet har de altid med sig — skibet — ligesom deres land: havet. Et skib ligner i det store og hele et andet, og havet er altid det samme. Mens deres omgivelser forbliver uforandrede, glider fremmede kyster, fremmede ansigter og livets skiftende umådelighed forbi. Det hele er tilsløret, ikke af mystik, men af en let foragtfuld uvidenhed. For en sømand er intet gådefuldt, måske bortset fra havet selv, der hersker over hans liv og er lige så uudgrundeligt som skæbnen. Ellers er en tilfældig spadseretur eller druktur i land efter arbejdstid nok til at åbenbare et helt kontinents hemmelighed for ham, og som regel synes han ikke, at hemmeligheden er værd at kende. Sømænds historier har en ligefrem enkelhed: Hele meningen ligger i skallen på en knækket nød. Men Marlow var ikke typisk, hvis man ser bort fra hans lyst til at fortælle historier. For ham lå en hændelses mening ikke indeni som en kerne, men udenom og omsluttede fortællingen. Fortællingen lod den kun træde frem, som et lysskær gør disen synlig, ligesom de tågede glorier, man undertiden ser i måneskinnets spøgelsesagtige lys.

changes.before: Hans bemærkning forekom slet ikke overraskende. Den var typisk for Marlow. Den blev modtaget i tavshed. Ingen gad så meget som grynte; og om lidt sagde han, meget langsomt — »Jeg tænkte på meget gamle tider, da romerne først kom her, for nitten hundrede år siden — forleden dag.... Lys er kommet ud af denne flod siden — du siger Riddere? Ja; men det er som en løbende ildflamme på en slette, som et lyn i skyerne. Vi lever i flimret — må det vare så længe den gamle jord bliver ved at rulle! Men mørke var her i går. Forestil dig følelserne hos en kommandant af en fin — hvad kalder I dem? — trireme på Middelhavet, der pludselig fik ordre til at gå mod nord; løbe over land tværs gennem Gallien i en fart; sat i kommando af et af disse fartøjer, legionærerne havde bygget — en vidunderlig flok handy mænd må de have været, også — vant til at bygge, åbenbart i hundredvis, på en måned eller to, hvis vi kan tro hvad vi læser. Forestil dig ham her — verdens ende, et hav i farve som bly, en himmel i farve som røg, en slags skib omtrent så stift som en harmonika — og sejlende op ad denne flod med forsyninger eller ordrer eller hvad du vil. Sandbanker, sumpe, skove, vilde, — kostbart lidt at spise egnet til en civiliseret mand, intet andet end Themse-vand at drikke. Ingen falernsk vin her, ingen gåen i land. Hist og her en militærlejr fortabt i en vildmark, som en nål i en høstak — kulde, tåge, storme, sygdom, eksil og død — død lurende i luften, i vandet, i krattet. De må være døde som fluer her. Åh, ja — han gjorde det. Gjorde det også meget vel, uden tvivl, og uden at tænke meget over det, undtagen bagefter for at prale af, hvad han havde gennemgået i sin tid, måske. De var mænd nok til at se mørket i øjnene. Og måske var han opmuntret ved at have øje for en chance for forfremmelse til flåden i Ravenna om en stund, hvis han havde gode venner i Rom og overlevede det forfærdelige klima. Eller tænk på en pæn ung borger i toga — måske for mange terninger, du ved — kommende herud i følge med en eller anden præfekt eller skatteopkræver, eller endda handelsmand, for at genoprette sin formue. Lande i en sump, marchere gennem skovene, og på en eller anden indenlandsk post mærke vildskaben, den totale vildskab, lukke sig om ham — alt det mystiske liv i vildmarken, der rører sig i skoven, i junglerne, i de vilde mænds hjerter. Der er ingen indvielse i den slags mysterier. Han må leve midt i det uforståelige, hvilket også er afskyeligt. Og det har også en fascination, som virker på ham. Fascinationen ved det afskyelige — du ved, forestil dig den voksende fortrydelse, længslen efter at flygte, den magtesløse afsky, overgivelsen, hadet.«
changes.after: Ingen syntes overrasket over hans bemærkning. Den lignede Marlow på en prik og blev modtaget i tavshed. Ingen gjorde sig den ulejlighed så meget som at grynte. Lidt efter sagde han meget langsomt: »Jeg tænkte på rigtig gamle dage, da romerne kom hertil første gang, for nitten hundrede år siden — forleden dag ... Siden er lyset kommet ud af denne flod — siger I riddere? Ja, men det er som en ild, der løber over en slette, som et lyn i skyerne. Vi lever i det flakkende lys — måtte det vare, så længe den gamle jord bliver ved med at dreje! Men mørket var her i går. Forestil jer, hvad kaptajnen på en fin — hvad er det, de hedder? — trireme i Middelhavet må have følt, når han pludselig blev sendt nordpå, i hast over land gennem Gallien, og fik kommandoen over et af de fartøjer, legionærerne byggede. De må have været en utrolig flok dygtige håndværkere, de legionærer; tilsyneladende byggede de hundredvis på en måned eller to, hvis vi skal tro det, vi læser. Forestil jer ham her, helt ude ved verdens ende, med et blyfarvet hav og en røgfarvet himmel, i et skib omtrent lige så stift som en harmonika, på vej op ad floden med forsyninger, ordrer eller hvad det nu var. Sandbanker, sumpe, skove, vilde — næsten intet at spise, som var egnet for et civiliseret menneske, og kun vand fra Themsen at drikke. Ingen falernervin her, ingen landlov. Hist og her en militærlejr fortabt i vildmarken som en nål i en høstak. Kulde, tåge, storme, sygdom, landflygtighed og død — døden på lur i luften, i vandet, i krattet. De må være døde som fluer her. Ja, han klarede det. Sikkert også godt, og uden at tænke meget over det, måske bortset fra bagefter, når han pralede af, hvad han havde været igennem. De var mænd nok til at møde mørket. Måske holdt han modet oppe ved at tænke på muligheden for en forfremmelse til flåden i Ravenna med tiden, hvis han havde gode venner i Rom og overlevede det forfærdelige klima. Eller forestil jer en pæn ung borger i toga — måske havde han spillet lidt for meget terning, ikke? — som kom herud i følget hos en præfekt, en skatteopkræver eller måske endda en handelsmand for at rette op på sin økonomi. Han går i land i en sump, marcherer gennem skovene og mærker på en station inde i landet, at vildskaben, den fuldstændige vildskab, har lukket sig om ham: hele vildmarkens gådefulde liv, der rører sig i skovene, i junglerne, i vilde menneskers hjerter. Man bliver heller ikke indviet i den slags mysterier. Han må leve midt i det uforståelige, som også er afskyeligt. Og det har en tiltrækning, som begynder at virke på ham. Afskyelighedens tiltrækning — forestil jer den voksende fortrydelse, længslen efter at slippe væk, den magtesløse afsky, overgivelsen, hadet.«

changes.before: »Jeg rejste på en fransk damper, og hun anløb hver eneste forbandet havn, de har derude, så vidt jeg kunne se, alene med det formål at sætte soldater og toldbetjente i land. Jeg betragtede kysten. At betragte en kyst, mens den glider forbi skibet, er som at tænke på en gåde. Der ligger den foran dig — smilende, rynkende panden, indbydende, storslået, lav, fad eller vild, og altid stum med en luft af at hviske, 'Kom og find ud af det.' Denne var næsten karakterløs, som om den stadig var under skabelse, med et udtryk af monoton barskhed. Kanten af en kolossal jungle, så mørkegrøn at den næsten var sort, kantet med hvid brænding, løb lige som en lineret streg, langt, langt væk langs et blåt hav, hvis glimmer blev sløret af en krybende tåge. Solen var hård, landet syntes at glinse og dryppe af damp. Hist og her dukkede gråligt-hvide pletter op samlet inden for den hvide brænding, med et flag der vajede over dem måske. Bosættelser nogle århundreder gamle, og stadig ikke større end nålehoveder på den uberørte vidde af deres baggrund. Vi bankede afsted, stoppede, satte soldater i land; fortsatte, satte toldkontorister i land for at opkræve afgift i, hvad der lignede en gudsforladt vildmark, med et blikskur og en flagstang fortabt i den; satte flere soldater i land — for at passe på toldkontoristerne, formoder jeg. Nogle, hørte jeg, druknede i brændingen; men om de gjorde eller ej, så syntes ingen at bekymre sig særligt. De blev bare smidt derude, og vi sejlede videre. Hver dag så kysten ens ud, som om vi ikke havde bevæget os; men vi passerede forskellige steder — handelssteder — med navne som Gran' Bassam, Little Popo; navne der syntes at høre til en eller anden sølle farce, der blev opført foran en uhyggelig bagvæg. En passagers lediggang, min isolation blandt alle disse mænd, som jeg ikke havde noget berøringspunkt med, det olierede og sløve hav, den ensartede dysterhed af kysten, syntes at holde mig væk fra tingenes sandhed, inde i en sørgmodig og meningsløs vrangforestillings slid. Brændingens stemme, hørt nu og da, var en positiv glæde, som en broders tale. Det var noget naturligt, der havde sin grund, der havde en mening. Nu og da gav en båd fra kysten et øjebliks kontakt med virkeligheden. Den blev padlet af sorte fyre. Man kunne langt borte se det hvide i deres øjenæbler glinse. De råbte, sang; deres kroppe strømmede af sved; de havde ansigter som groteske masker — disse fyre; men de havde knogle, muskel, en vild vitalitet, en intens energi i bevægelsen, der var lige så naturlig og sand som brændingen langs deres kyst. De behøvede ingen undskyldning for at være der. De var en stor trøst at se på. En tid følte jeg, at jeg stadig tilhørte en verden af ligefremme kendsgerninger; men følelsen varede ikke længe. Noget ville dukke op for at skræmme den væk. Engang, husker jeg, kom vi op til et krigsskib, der lå for anker ud for kysten. Der var ikke engang et skur der, og hun beskød krattet. Det viste sig, at franskmændene havde en af deres krige i gang derudefra. Hendes flag hang slapt som en klud; mundingerne af de lange seks-tommers kanoner stak frem overalt på det lave skrog; den fedtede, slimede dønning svingede hende dovent op og lod hende synke ned, gyngende hendes tynde master. I jordens, himlens og vandets tomme umådelighed, lå hun der, uforståelig, skyttende ind i et kontinent. Pop, ville en af seks-tommers kanonerne gå; en lille flamme ville fare ud og forsvinde, en lille hvid røg ville forsvinde, et lille projektil ville give et svagt skrig — og ingenting skete. Ingenting kunne ske. Der var et strejf af vanvid i forløbet, en fornemmelse af sørgelig komik i synet; og det blev ikke ophævet ved, at nogen om bord alvorligt forsikrede mig, at der var en lejr af indfødte — han kaldte dem fjender! — skjult ude af syne et eller andet sted.

changes.before: »Ingen grund til at fortælle jer meget om det. Nå, hvis en masse mystiske niggere bevæbnet med alle slags frygtelige våben pludselig begyndte at rejse på vejen mellem Deal og Gravesend, og fangede landfolkene til højre og venstre for at bære tunge byrder for dem, forestiller jeg mig, at hvert landbrug og hytte deromkring meget snart ville stå tomme. Jeg huskede den gamle læge — 'Det ville være interessant for videnskaben at iagttage de mentale forandringer hos individer på stedet.' Jeg følte, at jeg blev videnskabeligt interessant. changes.before: »Undskyld. Jeg glemte hjertesorgen, der udgør resten af prisen. Og hvad betyder prisen i virkeligheden, hvis tricket bliver godt udført? I gør jeres tricks meget godt. Og jeg gjorde det heller ikke skidt, eftersom jeg formåede ikke at sænke den dampbåd på min første tur. Det er stadig et under for mig. Forestil dig en blindfoldet mand sat til at køre en varevogn over en dårlig vej. Jeg svedte og rystede over den affære betydeligt, kan jeg sige dig. Trods alt, for en sømand er det at skrabe bunden af den ting, der formodes at flyde hele tiden under hans varetægt, den utilgivelige synd. Du husker det, du drømmer om det, du vågner om natten og tænker på det — år senere — og bliver varm og kold over hele kroppen. Jeg påstår ikke, at den dampbåd flød hele tiden. Og imellem måtte jeg holde øje med den vilde, der var fyrbøder. Han var et forbedret eksemplar; han kunne fyre op under en lodret kedel. changes.before: »Jeg gik fremad og beordrede kæden at blive hivet kort ind, så vi var klar til at slippe ankeret og bevæge dampbåden straks, hvis nødvendigt. 'Vil de angribe?' hviskede en ærefrygtfuld stemme. 'Vi vil alle blive slagtet i denne tåge,' mumlede en anden. Ansigterne trak sig under anspændelsen, hænderne rystede let, øjnene glemte at blinke. Det var meget kuriøst at se kontrasten mellem udtrykkene på de hvide mænd og de sorte fyre i vores besætning, der var lige så fremmede over for den del af floden som vi, selvom deres hjem kun var otte hundrede mil borte. De hvide, selvfølgelig meget urolige, havde desuden et kuriøst udtryk af at være smerteligt chokerede over en sådan oprørende larm. De andre havde et opmærksomt, naturligt interesseret udtryk; men deres ansigter var i bund og grund rolige, selv dem hos den ene eller to, der grinede, mens de halede i kæden. Flere udvekslede korte, grynt­ende fraser, som syntes at afgøre sagen til deres tilfredshed. Deres hovedmand, en ung, bredbrystet sort, alvorligt draperet i mørkeblå frynse-klæder, med vilde næsebor og sit hår alt sammen sat op kunstfærdigt i olierede ringe, stod nær mig. 'Aha!' sagde jeg, bare for kammeratskabs skyld. 'Fang 'em,' snerrede han, med en blodskudt udvidelse af øjnene og et glimt af skarpe tænder — 'fang 'em. Giv 'em til os.' 'Til jer, hva'?' spurgte jeg; 'hvad ville I gøre med dem?' 'Æd 'em!' sagde han kort, og lænede sin albue på rælingen og så ud i tågen i en værdig og dybt eftertænksom stilling. Jeg ville uden tvivl være blevet behørigt forfærdet, hvis det ikke var faldet mig ind, at han og hans fyre måtte være meget sultne: at de måtte være blevet stigende sultne i mindst denne sidste måned. De havde været hvervet i seks måneder (jeg tror ikke, at en eneste af dem havde nogen klar idé om tid, som vi i slutningen af utallige tidsaldre har. De tilhørte stadig tidens begyndelser — havde ingen nedarvet erfaring, der så at sige kunne lære dem), og selvfølgelig, så længe der var et stykke papir skrevet over i overensstemmelse med en eller anden farceagtig lov, der var lavet nede ved floden, faldt det ikke nogen ind at bekymre sig om, hvordan de skulle leve. De havde bestemt bragt med sig noget rådnet flodhest-kød, der ikke kan have holdt sig meget længe, alligevel, selv hvis pilgrimmene ikke, midt i en chokerende ballade, havde kastet en betragtelig mængde af det overbord. Det så ud som en overgreben handling; men det var virkelig et tilfælde af lovlig selvforsvar. Man kan ikke ånde død flodhest vågent, sovende og spisende, og samtidig bevare sit prekære greb om tilværelsen. Ud over det havde de fået hver uge tre stykker messingtråd, hver omkring ni tommer lange; og teorien var, at de skulle købe deres proviant med den valuta i flodbredsbyer. Du kan se, hvordan det virkede. Der var enten ingen landsbyer, eller folkene var fjendtlige, eller direktøren, som ligesom resten af os spiste ud af dåser med en lejlighedsvis gammel gedebuk kastet ind, ønskede ikke at stoppe damperen af en eller anden mere eller mindre obskur grund. Så medmindre de slugte tråden selv, eller lavede løkker af den til at fange fisk med, ser jeg ikke, hvad nytte deres ekstravagante løn kunne være for dem. Jeg må sige, den blev udbetalt med en regelmæssighed, der var en stor og ærværdig handelsvirksomhed værdig. For resten, det eneste at spise — selvom det ikke så spiseligt ud det mindste — jeg så i deres besiddelse var nogle klumper af et eller andet stof som halvkogt dej, af en snavset lavendelfarve, som de holdt indpakket i blade, og som de nu og da slugte et stykke af, men så lille, at det syntes gjort mere for tingens udseendes skyld end for noget seriøst formål om næring. Hvorfor i alle de gnavende sultens djævles navn de ikke gik efter os — de var tredive mod fem — og fik et godt måltid for én gangs skyld, forbavser mig nu, når jeg tænker på det. De var store kraftige mænd, med ikke meget kapacitet til at veje konsekvenserne, med mod, med styrke endnu, selvom deres hud ikke længere var blank og deres muskler ikke længere hårde. Og jeg så, at noget tilbageholdende, en af de menneskelige hemmeligheder, der forvirrer sandsynligheden, var trådt i kraft der. Jeg så på dem med en hurtig opvågning af interesse — ikke fordi det faldt mig ind, at jeg måske ville blive ædt af dem inden meget længe, selvom jeg indrømmer over for jer, at jeg netop da opfattede — i et nyt lys, så at sige — hvor usundt pilgrimmene så ud, og jeg håbede, ja, jeg håbede positivt, at min skikkelse ikke var så — hvad skal jeg sige? — så — uappetitlig: et strejf af fantastisk forfængelighed, der passede godt med drømme-fornemmelsen, der gennemtrængte alle mine dage på den tid. Måske havde jeg også en lille feber. Man kan ikke leve med fingeren evigt på pulsen. Jeg havde ofte 'en lille feber,' eller en lille smag af andre ting — vildmarkens legesyge poteslag, den forberedende leg før det mere alvorlige angreb, der kom i tide. Ja; jeg så på dem, som man ville se på enhver anden menneske, med en nysgerrighed over for deres impulser, motiver, kapaciteter, svagheder, når bragt til prøven af en ubønhørlig fysisk nødvendighed. Tilbageholdenhed! Hvilken mulig tilbageholdenhed? Var det overtro, afsky, tålmodighed, frygt — eller en eller anden form for primitiv ære? Ingen frygt kan stå mål med sult, ingen tålmodighed kan slide den ud, afsky eksisterer simpelthen ikke, hvor sult er; og hvad angår overtro, tro og det, du måske kalder principper, så er de mindre end avner i en brise. Kender du ikke djævelskaben ved langvarig sult, dens irriterende plage, dens sorte tanker, dens dystre og rugende ferocitet? Nå, det gør jeg. Det kræver al en mands medfødte styrke at bekæmpe sulten ordentligt. Det er virkelig lettere at se sorgen, vanæren og sjælens fortabelse i øjnene — end den slags langvarige sult. Trist, men sandt. Og disse fyre havde heller ikke nogen jordisk grund til nogen som helst form for skrupler. Tilbageholdenhed! Selvfølgelig kan man være for stor en tåbe til at fare vild, for sløv til overhovedet at vide, at mørkets magter angriber én. Jeg går ud fra, at ingen tåbe nogensinde har solgt sin sjæl til djævelen; tåben er for meget tåbe, eller djævelen for meget djævel — jeg ved ikke hvad. changes.before: “I looked at him, lost in astonishment. There he was before me, in motley, as though he had absconded from a troupe of mimes, enthusiastic, fabulous. His very existence was improbable, inexplicable, and altogether bewildering. He was an insoluble problem. It was inconceivable how he had existed, how he had succeeded in getting so far, how he had managed to remain—why he did not instantly disappear. ‘I went a little farther,’ he said, ‘then still a little farther—till I had gone so far that I don’t know how I’ll ever get back. Never mind. Plenty time. I can manage. You take Kurtz away quick—quick—I tell you.’ The glamour of youth enveloped his parti-coloured rags, his destitution, his loneliness, the essential desolation of his futile wanderings. For months—for years—his life hadn’t been worth a day’s purchase; and there he was gallantly, thoughtlessly alive, to all appearances indestructible solely by the virtue of his few years and of his unreflecting audacity. I was seduced into something like admiration—like envy. Glamour urged him on, glamour kept him unscathed. He surely wanted nothing from the wilderness but space to breathe in and to push on through. His need was to exist, and to move onwards at the greatest possible risk, and with a maximum of privation. If the absolutely pure, uncalculating, unpractical spirit of adventure had ever ruled a human being, it ruled this bepatched youth. I almost envied him the possession of this modest and clear flame. It seemed to have consumed all thought of self so completely, that even while he was talking to you, you forgot that it was he—the man before your eyes—who had gone through these things. I did not envy him his devotion to Kurtz, though. He had not meditated over it. It came to him, and he accepted it with a sort of eager fatalism. I must say that to me it appeared about the most dangerous thing in every way he had come upon so far.

changes.before: “On the contrary. It appears their intercourse had been very much broken by various causes. He had, as he informed me proudly, managed to nurse Kurtz through two illnesses (he alluded to it as you would to some risky feat), but as a rule Kurtz wandered alone, far in the depths of the forest. ‘Very often coming to this station, I had to wait days and days before he would turn up,’ he said. ‘Ah, it was worth waiting for!—sometimes.’ ‘What was he doing? exploring or what?’ I asked. ‘Oh, yes, of course’; he had discovered lots of villages, a lake, too—he did not know exactly in what direction; it was dangerous to inquire too much—but mostly his expeditions had been for ivory. ‘But he had no goods to trade with by that time,’ I objected. ‘There’s a good lot of cartridges left even yet,’ he answered, looking away. ‘To speak plainly, he raided the country,’ I said. He nodded. ‘Not alone, surely!’ He muttered something about the villages round that lake. ‘Kurtz got the tribe to follow him, did he?’ I suggested. He fidgeted a little. ‘They adored him,’ he said. The tone of these words was so extraordinary that I looked at him searchingly. It was curious to see his mingled eagerness and reluctance to speak of Kurtz. The man filled his life, occupied his thoughts, swayed his emotions. ‘What can you expect?’ he burst out; ‘he came to them with thunder and lightning, you know—and they had never seen anything like it—and very terrible. He could be very terrible. You can’t judge Mr. Kurtz as you would an ordinary man. No, no, no! Now—just to give you an idea—I don’t mind telling you, he wanted to shoot me, too, one day—but I don’t judge him.’ ‘Shoot you!’ I cried. ‘What for?’ ‘Well, I had a small lot of ivory the chief of that village near my house gave me. You see I used to shoot game for them. Well, he wanted it, and wouldn’t hear reason. He declared he would shoot me unless I gave him the ivory and then cleared out of the country, because he could do so, and had a fancy for it, and there was nothing on earth to prevent him killing whom he jolly well pleased. And it was true, too. I gave him the ivory. What did I care! But I didn’t clear out. No, no. I couldn’t leave him. I had to be careful, of course, till we got friendly again for a time. He had his second illness then. Afterwards I had to keep out of the way; but I didn’t mind. He was living for the most part in those villages on the lake. When he came down to the river, sometimes he would take to me, and sometimes it was better for me to be careful. This man suffered too much. He hated all this, and somehow he couldn’t get away. When I had a chance I begged him to try and leave while there was time; I offered to go back with him. And he would say yes, and then he would remain; go off on another ivory hunt; disappear for weeks; forget himself amongst these people—forget himself—you know.’ ‘Why! he’s mad,’ I said. He protested indignantly. Mr. Kurtz couldn’t be mad. If I had heard him talk, only two days ago, I wouldn’t dare hint at such a thing.... I had taken up my binoculars while we talked, and was looking at the shore, sweeping the limit of the forest at each side and at the back of the house. The consciousness of there being people in that bush, so silent, so quiet—as silent and quiet as the ruined house on the hill—made me uneasy. There was no sign on the face of nature of this amazing tale that was not so much told as suggested to me in desolate exclamations, completed by shrugs, in interrupted phrases, in hints ending in deep sighs. The woods were unmoved, like a mask—heavy, like the closed door of a prison—they looked with their air of hidden knowledge, of patient expectation, of unapproachable silence. The Russian was explaining to me that it was only lately that Mr. Kurtz had come down to the river, bringing along with him all the fighting men of that lake tribe. He had been absent for several months—getting himself adored, I suppose—and had come down unexpectedly, with the intention to all appearance of making a raid either across the river or down stream. Evidently the appetite for more ivory had got the better of the—what shall I say?—less material aspirations. However he had got much worse suddenly. ‘I heard he was lying helpless, and so I came up—took my chance,’ said the Russian. ‘Oh, he is bad, very bad.’ I directed my glass to the house. There were no signs of life, but there was the ruined roof, the long mud wall peeping above the grass, with three little square window-holes, no two of the same size; all this brought within reach of my hand, as it were. And then I made a brusque movement, and one of the remaining posts of that vanished fence leaped up in the field of my glass. You remember I told you I had been struck at the distance by certain attempts at ornamentation, rather remarkable in the ruinous aspect of the place. Now I had suddenly a nearer view, and its first result was to make me throw my head back as if before a blow. Then I went carefully from post to post with my glass, and I saw my mistake. These round knobs were not ornamental but symbolic; they were expressive and puzzling, striking and disturbing—food for thought and also for vultures if there had been any looking down from the sky; but at all events for such ants as were industrious enough to ascend the pole. They would have been even more impressive, those heads on the stakes, if their faces had not been turned to the house. Only one, the first I had made out, was facing my way. I was not so shocked as you may think. The start back I had given was really nothing but a movement of surprise. I had expected to see a knob of wood there, you know. I returned deliberately to the first I had seen—and there it was, black, dried, sunken, with closed eyelids—a head that seemed to sleep at the top of that pole, and, with the shrunken dry lips showing a narrow white line of the teeth, was smiling, too, smiling continuously at some endless and jocose dream of that eternal slumber.

changes.before: “‘I had immense plans,’ he muttered irresolutely. ‘Yes,’ said I; ‘but if you try to shout I’ll smash your head with—’ There was not a stick or a stone near. ‘I will throttle you for good,’ I corrected myself. ‘I was on the threshold of great things,’ he pleaded, in a voice of longing, with a wistfulness of tone that made my blood run cold. ‘And now for this stupid scoundrel—’ ‘Your success in Europe is assured in any case,’ I affirmed steadily. I did not want to have the throttling of him, you understand—and indeed it would have been very little use for any practical purpose. I tried to break the spell—the heavy, mute spell of the wilderness—that seemed to draw him to its pitiless breast by the awakening of forgotten and brutal instincts, by the memory of gratified and monstrous passions. This alone, I was convinced, had driven him out to the edge of the forest, to the bush, towards the gleam of fires, the throb of drums, the drone of weird incantations; this alone had beguiled his unlawful soul beyond the bounds of permitted aspirations. And, don’t you see, the terror of the position was not in being knocked on the head—though I had a very lively sense of that danger, too—but in this, that I had to deal with a being to whom I could not appeal in the name of anything high or low. I had, even like the niggers, to invoke him—himself—his own exalted and incredible degradation. There was nothing either above or below him, and I knew it. He had kicked himself loose of the earth. Confound the man! he had kicked the very earth to pieces. He was alone, and I before him did not know whether I stood on the ground or floated in the air. I’ve been telling you what we said—repeating the phrases we pronounced—but what’s the good? They were common everyday words—the familiar, vague sounds exchanged on every waking day of life. But what of that? They had behind them, to my mind, the terrific suggestiveness of words heard in dreams, of phrases spoken in nightmares. Soul! If anybody ever struggled with a soul, I am the man. And I wasn’t arguing with a lunatic either. Believe me or not, his intelligence was perfectly clear—concentrated, it is true, upon himself with horrible intensity, yet clear; and therein was my only chance—barring, of course, the killing him there and then, which wasn’t so good, on account of unavoidable noise. But his soul was mad. Being alone in the wilderness, it had looked within itself, and, by heavens! I tell you, it had gone mad. I had—for my sins, I suppose—to go through the ordeal of looking into it myself. No eloquence could have been so withering to one’s belief in mankind as his final burst of sincerity. He struggled with himself, too. I saw it—I heard it. I saw the inconceivable mystery of a soul that knew no restraint, no faith, and no fear, yet struggling blindly with itself. I kept my head pretty well; but when I had him at last stretched on the couch, I wiped my forehead, while my legs shook under me as though I had carried half a ton on my back down that hill. And yet I had only supported him, his bony arm clasped round my neck—and he was not much heavier than a child.

changes.before: “When next day we left at noon, the crowd, of whose presence behind the curtain of trees I had been acutely conscious all the time, flowed out of the woods again, filled the clearing, covered the slope with a mass of naked, breathing, quivering, bronze bodies. changes.before: “However, as you see, I did not go to join Kurtz there and then. I did not. I remained to dream the nightmare out to the end, and to show my loyalty to Kurtz once more. Destiny. My destiny! Droll thing life is—that mysterious arrangement of merciless logic for a futile purpose. The most you can hope from it is some knowledge of yourself—that comes too late—a crop of unextinguishable regrets. I have wrestled with death. It is the most unexciting contest you can imagine. It takes place in an impalpable greyness, with nothing underfoot, with nothing around, without spectators, without clamour, without glory, without the great desire of victory, without the great fear of defeat, in a sickly atmosphere of tepid scepticism, without much belief in your own right, and still less in that of your adversary. If such is the form of ultimate wisdom, then life is a greater riddle than some of us think it to be. I was within a hair’s breadth of the last opportunity for pronouncement, and I found with humiliation that probably I would have nothing to say. This is the reason why I affirm that Kurtz was a remarkable man. He had something to say. He said it. Since I had peeped over the edge myself, I understand better the meaning of his stare, that could not see the flame of the candle, but was wide enough to embrace the whole universe, piercing enough to penetrate all the hearts that beat in the darkness. He had summed up—he had judged. ‘The horror!’ He was a remarkable man. After all, this was the expression of some sort of belief; it had candour, it had conviction, it had a vibrating note of revolt in its whisper, it had the appalling face of a glimpsed truth—the strange commingling of desire and hate. And it is not my own extremity I remember best—a vision of greyness without form filled with physical pain, and a careless contempt for the evanescence of all things—even of this pain itself. No! It is his extremity that I seem to have lived through. True, he had made that last stride, he had stepped over the edge, while I had been permitted to draw back my hesitating foot. And perhaps in this is the whole difference; perhaps all the wisdom, and all truth, and all sincerity, are just compressed into that inappreciable moment of time in which we step over the threshold of the invisible. Perhaps! I like to think my summing-up would not have been a word of careless contempt. Better his cry—much better. It was an affirmation, a moral victory paid for by innumerable defeats, by abominable terrors, by abominable satisfactions. But it was a victory! That is why I have remained loyal to Kurtz to the last, and even beyond, when a long time after I heard once more, not his own voice, but the echo of his magnificent eloquence thrown to me from a soul as translucently pure as a cliff of crystal.
changes.after: »Men som I ser, fulgte jeg ikke Kurtz dengang. Det gjorde jeg ikke. Jeg blev tilbage for at drømme mareridtet til ende og endnu en gang vise min troskab mod Kurtz. Skæbnen. Min skæbne! Livet er en pudsig ting, dette gådefulde arrangement af ubarmhjertig logik til et formålsløst formål. Det meste, man kan håbe at få ud af det, er lidt viden om sig selv, som kommer for sent, en høst af uudslukkelig fortrydelse. Jeg har kæmpet med døden. Det er den mindst spændende kamp, man kan forestille sig. Den foregår i et uhåndgribeligt gråt rum, med intet under fødderne og intet omkring sig, uden tilskuere, uden larm, uden ære, uden det store ønske om sejr, uden den store frygt for nederlag, i en sygelig atmosfære af lunken skepsis, uden megen tro på ens egen ret og endnu mindre på modstanderens. changes.before: “No, they did not bury me, though there is a period of time which I remember mistily, with a shuddering wonder, like a passage through some inconceivable world that had no hope in it and no desire. I found myself back in the sepulchral city resenting the sight of people hurrying through the streets to filch a little money from each other, to devour their infamous cookery, to gulp their unwholesome beer, to dream their insignificant and silly dreams. They trespassed upon my thoughts. They were intruders whose knowledge of life was to me an irritating pretence, because I felt so sure they could not possibly know the things I knew. Their bearing, which was simply the bearing of commonplace individuals going about their business in the assurance of perfect safety, was offensive to me like the outrageous flauntings of folly in the face of a danger it is unable to comprehend. I had no particular desire to enlighten them, but I had some difficulty in restraining myself from laughing in their faces so full of stupid importance. I daresay I was not very well at that time. I tottered about the streets—there were various affairs to settle—grinning bitterly at perfectly respectable persons. I admit my behaviour was inexcusable, but then my temperature was seldom normal in these days. My dear aunt’s endeavours to ‘nurse up my strength’ seemed altogether beside the mark. It was not my strength that wanted nursing, it was my imagination that wanted soothing. I kept the bundle of papers given me by Kurtz, not knowing exactly what to do with it. His mother had died lately, watched over, as I was told, by his Intended. A clean-shaved man, with an official manner and wearing gold-rimmed spectacles, called on me one day and made inquiries, at first circuitous, afterwards suavely pressing, about what he was pleased to denominate certain ‘documents.’ I was not surprised, because I had had two rows with the manager on the subject out there. I had refused to give up the smallest scrap out of that package, and I took the same attitude with the spectacled man. He became darkly menacing at last, and with much heat argued that the Company had the right to every bit of information about its ‘territories.’ And said he, ‘Mr. Kurtz’s knowledge of unexplored regions must have been necessarily extensive and peculiar—owing to his great abilities and to the deplorable circumstances in which he had been placed: therefore—’ I assured him Mr. Kurtz’s knowledge, however extensive, did not bear upon the problems of commerce or administration. He invoked then the name of science. ‘It would be an incalculable loss if,’ etc., etc. I offered him the report on the ‘Suppression of Savage Customs,’ with the postscriptum torn off. He took it up eagerly, but ended by sniffing at it with an air of contempt. ‘This is not what we had a right to expect,’ he remarked. ‘Expect nothing else,’ I said. ‘There are only private letters.’ He withdrew upon some threat of legal proceedings, and I saw him no more; but another fellow, calling himself Kurtz’s cousin, appeared two days later, and was anxious to hear all the details about his dear relative’s last moments. Incidentally he gave me to understand that Kurtz had been essentially a great musician. ‘There was the making of an immense success,’ said the man, who was an organist, I believe, with lank grey hair flowing over a greasy coat-collar. I had no reason to doubt his statement; and to this day I am unable to say what was Kurtz’s profession, whether he ever had any—which was the greatest of his talents. I had taken him for a painter who wrote for the papers, or else for a journalist who could paint—but even the cousin (who took snuff during the interview) could not tell me what he had been—exactly. He was a universal genius—on that point I agreed with the old chap, who thereupon blew his nose noisily into a large cotton handkerchief and withdrew in senile agitation, bearing off some family letters and memoranda without importance. Ultimately a journalist anxious to know something of the fate of his ‘dear colleague’ turned up. This visitor informed me Kurtz’s proper sphere ought to have been politics ‘on the popular side.’ He had furry straight eyebrows, bristly hair cropped short, an eyeglass on a broad ribbon, and, becoming expansive, confessed his opinion that Kurtz really couldn’t write a bit—‘but heavens! how that man could talk. He electrified large meetings. He had faith—don’t you see?—he had the faith. He could get himself to believe anything—anything. He would have been a splendid leader of an extreme party.’ ‘What party?’ I asked. ‘Any party,’ answered the other. ‘He was an—an—extremist.’ Did I not think so? I assented. Did I know, he asked, with a sudden flash of curiosity, ‘what it was that had induced him to go out there?’ ‘Yes,’ said I, and forthwith handed him the famous Report for publication, if he thought fit. He glanced through it hurriedly, mumbling all the time, judged ‘it would do,’ and took himself off with this plunder.

Deres optræden, som blot var almindelige menneskers optræden, mens de passede deres gøremål i fuld forvisning om at være sikre, krænkede mig som dårskabens skamløse opvisning over for en fare, den ikke kan begribe. Jeg havde ingen særlig lyst til at oplyse dem, men havde svært ved at lade være med at le dem op i deres dumt selvhøjtidelige ansigter. Jeg var nok ikke helt rask dengang. Det var ikke mine kræfter, der behøvede pleje, men min fantasi, der behøvede ro. Jeg beholdt den pakke papirer, Kurtz havde givet mig, uden rigtigt at vide, hvad jeg skulle stille op med den. Hans mor var død for nylig, passet, fik jeg at vide, af hans forlovede. En glatbarberet mand med embedsmandsmanerer og guldindfattede briller besøgte mig en dag og spurgte, først ad omveje, siden høfligt påtrængende, til det, han behagede at kalde visse ›dokumenter‹. Det overraskede mig ikke, for jeg havde haft to skænderier med bestyreren om emnet derude. Jeg tilbød ham rapporten om ›Bekæmpelse af Vilde Skikke‹ med efterskriften revet af. I forbifarten lod han mig forstå, at Kurtz i grunden havde været en stor musiker. ›Han havde alt, hvad der skulle til for en enorm succes,‹ sagde manden, som vist var organist, med langt, slapt gråt hår ned over en fedtet frakkekrave. Jeg havde taget ham for en maler, der skrev i aviserne, eller en journalist, der kunne male, men selv fætteren, som tog snus under samtalen, kunne ikke fortælle mig, hvad han præcis havde været. Han var et universalgeni; på det punkt var jeg enig med den gamle mand, som derefter pudsede næsen højlydt i et stort bomuldslommetørklæde og gik sin vej i senil ophidselse med nogle familiebreve og uvæsentlige notater. Han elektriserede store forsamlinger. Han havde tro, forstår De, han havde troen. Han kunne få sig selv til at tro på hvad som helst — hvad som helst. Vidste jeg, spurgte han med et pludseligt glimt af nysgerrighed, ›hvad der havde fået ham til at rejse derud?‹ ›Ja,‹ sagde jeg og rakte ham straks den berømte rapport, så han kunne offentliggøre den, hvis han fandt det passende. changes.before: “Thus I was left at last with a slim packet of letters and the girl’s portrait. She struck me as beautiful—I mean she had a beautiful expression. I know that the sunlight can be made to lie, too, yet one felt that no manipulation of light and pose could have conveyed the delicate shade of truthfulness upon those features. She seemed ready to listen without mental reservation, without suspicion, without a thought for herself. I concluded I would go and give her back her portrait and those letters myself. Curiosity? Yes; and also some other feeling perhaps. All that had been Kurtz’s had passed out of my hands: his soul, his body, his station, his plans, his ivory, his career. There remained only his memory and his Intended—and I wanted to give that up, too, to the past, in a way—to surrender personally all that remained of him with me to that oblivion which is the last word of our common fate. I don’t defend myself. I had no clear perception of what it was I really wanted. Perhaps it was an impulse of unconscious loyalty, or the fulfilment of one of those ironic necessities that lurk in the facts of human existence. I don’t know. I can’t tell. But I went.

changes.before: “I thought his memory was like the other memories of the dead that accumulate in every man’s life—a vague impress on the brain of shadows that had fallen on it in their swift and final passage; but before the high and ponderous door, between the tall houses of a street as still and decorous as a well-kept alley in a cemetery, I had a vision of him on the stretcher, opening his mouth voraciously, as if to devour all the earth with all its mankind. He lived then before me; he lived as much as he had ever lived—a shadow insatiable of splendid appearances, of frightful realities; a shadow darker than the shadow of the night, and draped nobly in the folds of a gorgeous eloquence. The vision seemed to enter the house with me—the stretcher, the phantom-bearers, the wild crowd of obedient worshippers, the gloom of the forests, the glitter of the reach between the murky bends, the beat of the drum, regular and muffled like the beating of a heart—the heart of a conquering darkness. It was a moment of triumph for the wilderness, an invading and vengeful rush which, it seemed to me, I would have to keep back alone for the salvation of another soul. And the memory of what I had heard him say afar there, with the horned shapes stirring at my back, in the glow of fires, within the patient woods, those broken phrases came back to me, were heard again in their ominous and terrifying simplicity. I remembered his abject pleading, his abject threats, the colossal scale of his vile desires, the meanness, the torment, the tempestuous anguish of his soul. And later on I seemed to see his collected languid manner, when he said one day, ‘This lot of ivory now is really mine. The Company did not pay for it. I collected it myself at a very great personal risk. I am afraid they will try to claim it as theirs though. H’m. It is a difficult case. What do you think I ought to do—resist? Eh? I want no more than justice.’... He wanted no more than justice—no more than justice. I rang the bell before a mahogany door on the first floor, and while I waited he seemed to stare at me out of the glassy panel—stare with that wide and immense stare embracing, condemning, loathing all the universe. I seemed to hear the whispered cry, “The horror! The horror!”

It was more than a year since his death, more than a year since the news came; she seemed as though she would remember and mourn forever. She took both my hands in hers and murmured, ‘I had heard you were coming.’ I noticed she was not very young—I mean not girlish. She had a mature capacity for fidelity, for belief, for suffering. The room seemed to have grown darker, as if all the sad light of the cloudy evening had taken refuge on her forehead. This fair hair, this pale visage, this pure brow, seemed surrounded by an ashy halo from which the dark eyes looked out at me. Their glance was guileless, profound, confident, and trustful. She carried her sorrowful head as though she were proud of that sorrow, as though she would say, ‘I—I alone know how to mourn for him as he deserves.’ But while we were still shaking hands, such a look of awful desolation came upon her face that I perceived she was one of those creatures that are not the playthings of Time. For her he had died only yesterday. And, by Jove! the impression was so powerful that for me, too, he seemed to have died only yesterday—nay, this very minute. I saw her and him in the same instant of time—his death and her sorrow—I saw her sorrow in the very moment of his death. Do you understand? I saw them together—I heard them together. She had said, with a deep catch of the breath, ‘I have survived’ while my strained ears seemed to hear distinctly, mingled with her tone of despairing regret, the summing up whisper of his eternal condemnation. I asked myself what I was doing there, with a sensation of panic in my heart as though I had blundered into a place of cruel and absurd mysteries not fit for a human being to behold.
